# The Thirty-Seven Letters of Monk Hideo, As Compiled by His Opponent

**Edited, with annotations, by Arakawa Shin'ichi**

Published posthumously by arrangement with the Eiheiji Press

---

## Editor's Preface

The Twelfth All-Japan Sword Forms Championship was held on August 3, 1981, in the municipal gymnasium at Nara. Temperatures inside the gymnasium reached forty-one degrees by the afternoon session. Eight hundred spectators were present. The final match was between Hideo Takashi, then thirty-four, the defending champion and widely regarded as the finest swordsman of his generation, and myself, then thirty-one, ranked second.

We bowed. We assumed our stances. The timekeeper raised his flag.

Hideo looked at me. I have tried, many times, to describe the expression on his face in that moment. It was not anguish. It was not serenity. In later years I sometimes thought it resembled the expression of a man who has just finished a very long calculation and is checking his answer for the last time. But that is not right either.

He lowered his bokken. He set it on the floor. He straightened, bowed—not to me, but to the panel—and walked out through the athletes' entrance. I heard his bare feet on the concrete corridor. Then I could not hear them anymore.

The judges convened for eleven minutes. I was declared champion.

I carried something away from that gymnasium. It was not a trophy—I received one, and it sat in my dojo for thirty years, and I could describe its dimensions and engraving to you now, but that is not what I carried. What I carried was lighter and heavier than the trophy, and I have not set it down.

I am sixty-nine years old. My physician tells me what physicians tell men of sixty-nine when they have news to deliver, and I have received it with the composure I hope I have demonstrated throughout my life in budō. I mention this only because it bears on the question of why I am publishing these letters now, and not before, and not never. A dying man is permitted certain acts that would, in a living man, require justification. I offer none.

What follows are thirty-seven letters sent to me by Hideo over the course of forty years, from 1981 until his death in 2021. I never solicited them. I answered none of them. I have arranged them in chronological order and provided annotations where I believed context might be useful to a reader unfamiliar with our tradition, our art, or the particular history of two men who met once in competition and never again in the flesh.

Whether these letters explain what happened on August 3, 1981, I will leave to the reader. I have had forty years to decide and have not.

—A.S.
Kamakura, October 2022

---

## Letter One

*Received September 1981. Paper: standard stationery, commercially available. Postmarked Fukui Prefecture.*

Arakawa-san,

I arrived at Eiheiji on the twentieth of August. The journey from Nara took four days by train and bus, though it could have been done in one. I was not in a hurry. Or rather, I was in the kind of hurry that expresses itself as slowness—the need to arrive somewhere absolute, which makes every intermediate step feel like a delay that must be endured with the whole body.

The monastery is cold even in summer. My cell measures two tatami mats. There is a window that faces north and admits a quality of light I have not encountered before—pale, definitive, the light of a place that has decided what it is. I wake at three-thirty for the morning service. My hands, which have held a bokken since I was eleven, now hold a broom.

A bird has built a nest above my window. I do not know what kind. It is brown and very small and it repeats one phrase with the persistence of a man who believes that if he can only say the thing precisely enough, the world will rearrange itself around the saying.

I do not know why I am writing to you. Perhaps because you are the last person who saw me as I was before I became what I am now. That seems like a thing worth acknowledging, even if I cannot yet say what it means.

With respect,
Hideo

**[Annotation, A.S.]:** I received this letter at my apartment in Osaka, where I was living while establishing my dojo. I had signed a lease on a commercial space in the Tennōji district three days earlier. The deposit was paid with prize money from the championship. I remember reading this letter standing in my kitchen and then placing it in a drawer. I did not think about it again for some time.

---

## Letter Two

*Received January 1982. Paper: handmade washi, likely produced at the monastery. Postmarked Fukui Prefecture.*

Arakawa-san,

Winter here is a physical argument. The snow does not fall so much as accumulate, like evidence. My cell door freezes shut some mornings and must be struck with the heel of the hand—a motion that amuses me for reasons I will not explain, since you would not find them amusing.

The schedule is invariant. Zazen at three-forty-five. Chanting at five. Cleaning, breakfast, work, more zazen, more chanting, sleep. The repetition is the practice, the monks tell me. I am learning to believe them, by which I mean I am learning to stop needing to believe them, which they tell me is the same thing.

I eat rice and pickled vegetables. I swept the main hall for three hours yesterday and was told I swept it poorly. I swept it again. I was told this was also poor. I swept it a third time and was told nothing, which I have learned to interpret as the highest available praise.

I hope your winter is milder.

Hideo

**[Annotation, A.S.]:** My dojo opened in November 1981. Fourteen students enrolled in the first month, which exceeded my expectations. Several had traveled from other cities. One, a young man named Ogawa, told me during his intake interview that he had attended the championship at Nara and had been so impressed by my form that he abandoned his previous instructor. I mention this because it represents a pattern that would continue for many years: students came to me because of what they had witnessed on August 3, or because of what others told them they had witnessed. My reputation was built on a single afternoon. This is not unusual in budō. A career in martial arts is, in some sense, the elaboration of a single moment of demonstrated truth. I taught Ogawa for nine years. He became a fine swordsman.

---

## Letter Three

*Received April 1982. Paper: washi, as before. A pressed wildflower—campion, I believe—was enclosed, and has been preserved between the pages.*

Arakawa-san,

Spring arrives here the way understanding arrives in zazen—not gradually, but all at once, in a rush that retroactively makes the waiting feel purposeful. Yesterday the plum trees along the entrance path opened, and the monks who have been here for decades stopped to look at them with the same amazement as the monks who arrived last week. I find this encouraging. It suggests that certain forms of astonishment are not subject to erosion.

I have been assigned to the kitchen. My teacher, an elderly monk named Ryōnen, oversees the preparation of meals with a seriousness that would seem excessive if applied to anything less essential. He corrected my grip on a kitchen knife yesterday—a lateral adjustment of perhaps two millimeters—and I felt the correction in my entire body, the way one feels a single degree of deviation in a compass bearing only after walking far enough for the error to compound.

I am beginning to understand something about precision that I thought I already understood. In competition, precision is a means. Here, precision is a climate.

The campion is for no reason. I saw it and thought you might like to see it.

Hideo

**[Annotation, A.S.]:** The campion has retained its color reasonably well. I have never had a particular interest in flowers.

I should note, for the sake of transparency, that by the spring of 1982 I had been invited to teach seminars in Kyoto, Hiroshima, and Sendai. The Japanese Budō Federation published a profile of my technique in their quarterly journal, focusing on what they called the "Arakawa stance"—a right-forward guard I had employed throughout the tournament, characterized by an open hip rotation and a high rear hand. This stance became the foundation of my teaching method. I still believe it to be technically sound.

---

## Letter Four

*Received August 1982. Paper: washi. Postmarked Fukui Prefecture.*

Arakawa-san,

One year.

The anniversary is meaningless, of course. The monastery does not observe personal calendars. But the body observes what the mind renounces, and today my body remembered August, and heat, and the particular quality of gymnasium light, which is the light of a place that has not decided what it is.

I sat with this for a long time during morning zazen. Ryōnen, who has a talent for appearing beside you at the moment you most wish to be unobserved, asked me afterward what I had been sitting with. I told him: a gymnasium. He asked if it was empty or full. I said full. He said, "Sit with it until it is empty. Then sit with the emptiness. That is the harder practice."

I am learning that monks give advice the way stones give heat—slowly, and long after the fire that warmed them has gone out.

Hideo

**[Annotation, A.S.]:** I did not observe the anniversary. I was teaching an afternoon class when it passed. It is likely that I was in the middle of demonstrating the opening transition of the stance, which requires the practitioner to shift weight to the rear foot while maintaining the appearance of forward intention. This is the most misunderstood element of the technique: several of my early students would rush the transition, collapsing into it rather than settling. The distinction is subtle but consequential.

---

## Letter Five

*Received February 1983. Paper: washi, thinner than previous letters. Ink appears to have been ground by hand.*

Arakawa-san,

Snow again. I am told it is milder this year, but I lack the experience to confirm. Each winter so far has been the only winter.

A new monk arrived last week, a young man who had been a judoka of some distinction. He moves through the monastery with the compressed energy of an athlete who has not yet learned to release the habit of readiness. I recognize it. I wore it for months. Ryōnen has assigned him to the garden, which is mostly frozen, and I think the assignment is deliberate—there is nothing to defend against in a frozen garden, and eventually the body learns this and allows itself a different posture.

I have been reading the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. Huineng writes that the original mind is like a mirror—clear, reflective, already perfect. Our work is not to polish it but to stop obscuring it. I find this difficult to accept, perhaps because in budō we are trained to believe that the unworked thing is always inferior to the worked one. That a stance must be refined, a cut must be practiced ten thousand times, a flaw must be corrected.

But what if the correction introduces the flaw? What if the ten-thousandth repetition is the one that takes you farthest from the thing you were trying to reach?

I am circling something. Forgive the circles.

Hideo

**[Annotation, A.S.]:** The question Hideo raises here concerning repetition and refinement is a common one in contemplative traditions, though it takes a particular form in martial arts, where the stakes of imprecision are not abstract. A flawed meditation posture may slow one's progress. A flawed sword technique may cost a life—or, in our modern context, a match, a title, a career. The distinction is not trivial.

I relocated my dojo in 1983, from Tennōji to a larger space in Kita-ku. The new location was in a part of the city where the championship at Nara was not well known. I chose it for the space—it could accommodate thirty students, and I had outgrown the Tennōji studio—and for the parking, which my students had requested. I mention this for practical context only.

---

## Letter Six

*Received July 1983. Paper: washi. A small ink drawing of a bird accompanies the text—I believe it is the bird from the first letter, or its descendant.*

Arakawa-san,

The bird is back, or its child is. I cannot tell. It sings the same phrase. Persistence or inheritance—the effect is identical.

I assisted at an ordination ceremony yesterday. The initiate, a woman of about fifty, had been a schoolteacher for twenty-five years. During the head-shaving, her face passed through an expression I recognized from somewhere I could not place—not sorrow, not relief, but the look of a person who is watching something become irrevocable and has chosen not to intervene. I thought about it for the rest of the day. By evening I remembered where I had seen it. But this letter is too short for that.

The heat is extraordinary. It sits on the monastery like a hand.

Hideo

**[Annotation, A.S.]:** No annotation.

---

## Letter Seven

*Received November 1983. Paper: washi, heavier stock. Written in a single sitting, I believe—the ink consistency is uniform throughout, which is unusual for Hideo's letters; most show evidence of multiple sessions.*

Arakawa-san,

I owe you an explanation for the brevity of my last letter. Or rather, I owe you an explanation for its incompleteness. I began to say something and drew back, and I think you deserve to know, at the very least, that I drew back—that the retreat was deliberate, not accidental.

I will try again.

There is a practice exercise Ryōnen uses with newer monks, a kind of walking meditation in which two monks face each other and advance along a corridor. The corridor is narrow—shoulder-width—and the two monks must pass without touching. There is always enough room, but the mind refuses to believe this, and the body, obedient to the mind's refusal, tenses and twists and creates the very collision it feared.

Ryōnen asked me to demonstrate the exercise with a senior monk, Brother Daichi, who is seventy-three and moves with the unhurried precision of water finding its level. As we approached each other in the corridor, I saw—I *felt*—the exact angle at which his left shoulder was vulnerable. Not to harm. Not in any practical sense. But in the way a swordsman sees openings: involuntarily, the way the eye sees color. His robe hung in such a way that his balance point was legible, and I knew—I knew in my hands, not in my mind—that a lateral step and a quarter-rotation would pass through his center as cleanly as a brush through ink.

I did not step. I did not rotate. We passed each other in the corridor and he smiled at me and the exercise was completed. Ryōnen said nothing, which meant it was correct.

But afterward I sat in my cell and asked myself: is it merciful, what I did not do? Or is there something else—something that precedes mercy—in the act of *seeing* what could be done and *choosing* to seal it inside the seeing? Is the seeing itself a kind of violence? And if so, is the silence that preserves it a second kind?

I am aware that this is abstract. I am aware that I am still circling. The circle is smaller now. I do not know if that constitutes progress or simply a tighter confinement.

Hideo
